result: Neonatal dorsal and intermediate/ventral hippocampus exhibit distinct patterns of theta burst activity. i/vHP shows higher occurrence (8.1±0.2 vs 5.2±0.3 oscillations/min, p<0.001), larger amplitude (110.6±5.6 vs 92.9±2.6 µV, p=0.015), and shorter duration (3.5±0.1 vs 4.3±0.1 s, p<0.001) of theta bursts compared to dHP. However, theta band power is stronger in dHP (13.0±1.3 vs 10.3±0.5, p=0.026), while beta and gamma band powers are similar between regions.
evaluation: Claims C1-C6 provide comprehensive quantitative characterization of oscillatory activity differences along the septo-temporal axis with appropriate statistical testing (n=103 mice for i/vHP, n=41 for dHP). The findings are internally consistent and supported by spectral analysis data shown in Figure 1. Sample sizes are adequate and statistical significance is properly reported with p-values.

result: Sharp-wave and ripple activity differs along the hippocampal septo-temporal axis. Pyramidal neurons in i/vHP fire at higher rates (0.45±0.01 vs 0.35±0.02 Hz, p=0.025). SPWs are more prominent in dHP (712.8±31.5 vs 223.8±6.3 µV, p<0.001) but occur more frequently in i/vHP (8.6±0.2 vs 6.6±0.5, p<0.001). Ripple power and ripple-related spiking are stronger in dHP.
evaluation: Claims C7-C11 demonstrate consistent patterns of SPW-ripple differences with appropriate statistical testing. The inverse relationship between SPW amplitude (higher in dHP) and occurrence (higher in i/vHP) is well-documented with adequate sample sizes (n=557 units from i/vHP, n=158 from dHP for firing rates). All measurements include proper statistical comparisons.

result: Intermediate/ventral hippocampus shows stronger functional coupling with prelimbic cortex than dorsal hippocampus. PL-i/vHP coherence is higher across all frequency bands compared to PL-dHP. Directed information flow (gPDC) from i/vHP to PL (0.069±0.003) is significantly stronger than from dHP to PL (0.053±0.003, p<0.001), specifically in theta frequency range. Phase-locking analysis shows 20% of prelimbic units locked to i/vHP theta versus only 6.5% to dHP theta.
evaluation: Claims C12-C17 provide converging evidence from multiple analytical approaches (coherence, gPDC, phase-locking) demonstrating stronger i/vHP-PL coupling. The use of imaginary coherence (C91) appropriately controls for volume conduction artifacts. Sample sizes are adequate and statistical tests are properly applied. The frequency-specific nature of the effect (theta but not beta, C16) strengthens the interpretation.

result: SPWs-ripples from i/vHP induce stronger prelimbic activation than those from dHP. Prelimbic oscillatory power increases significantly more after i/vHP SPWs across theta (249.5±14.5 vs 186.9±12.5 µV², p=0.0088), beta (48.1±2.8 vs 34.3±3.3 µV², p=0.0049), and gamma (17.4±1.2 vs 11.3±0.9 µV², p=0.0026) bands. Prelimbic firing peaks ~90 ms after i/vHP SPWs and remains elevated for several seconds.
evaluation: Claims C18-C19 and C90 demonstrate temporal relationships between hippocampal SPWs and prelimbic responses with appropriate statistical testing. The ~100 ms delay is consistent with monosynaptic or short polysynaptic transmission. Power analysis across multiple frequency bands provides comprehensive characterization. Sample sizes are adequate (n=41 for dHP, n=103 for i/vHP).

result: Anatomical tracing reveals dense direct projections from i/vHP CA1 to prelimbic cortex. Retrograde tracing shows significantly higher density of projection neurons in i/vHP (3.29×10³±0.19×10³ cells/mm²) compared to dHP (0.15×10³±0.074×10³ cells/mm², p<0.001). Anterograde tracing confirms axonal projections from i/vHP to PL layers V and VI in 7 of 9 mice.
evaluation: Claims C20-C21 provide anatomical evidence supporting functional connectivity differences. Both retrograde (Fluorogold) and anterograde (BDA) tracing methods converge on the same conclusion. The >20-fold difference in projection neuron density is statistically robust. The success rate for anterograde tracing (7/9 mice) is reasonable for this technique.

result: In utero electroporation successfully transfects pyramidal neurons in hippocampal CA1 without affecting normal development. Transfection efficiency is 18.3±1.0% in dHP and 14.5±1.5% in i/vHP. Cell-type specificity is confirmed by morphology and absence of GABA staining. IUE reduces litter size (4.5±0.5 vs 6.5±0.7 pups/litter, p=0.017) but does not affect somatic growth parameters or reflexes.
evaluation: Claims C22-C26 establish the validity of the optogenetic approach. Transfection efficiency is quantified with adequate sample sizes (n=36 slices from 13 mice for dHP, n=12 slices from 11 mice for i/vHP). Cell-type specificity is verified through multiple methods (morphology, GABA immunostaining). Developmental controls are appropriate, though the litter size reduction is a notable limitation that is properly reported.

result: Optogenetic activation of i/vHP pyramidal neurons at 8 Hz, but not 4 or 16 Hz, causally drives prelimbic oscillations. Light stimulation (473 nm, 20-40 mW/mm²) evokes precisely timed firing (<10 ms latency) in both dHP and i/vHP. Only 8 Hz stimulation of i/vHP significantly increases prelimbic power across theta (p=0.039), beta (p=0.030), and gamma (p=0.0036) bands. dHP stimulation and opsin-free controls show no effects.
evaluation: Claims C27-C31 provide causal evidence for i/vHP driving prelimbic activity with appropriate controls (dHP stimulation, opsin-free animals, multiple frequencies). The frequency-specificity (8 Hz but not 4 or 16 Hz) is a critical finding supported by statistical testing. Sample sizes are adequate (n=22 for dHP, n=9 for i/vHP). The lack of effect from dHP stimulation despite successful neuronal activation strengthens the conclusion about anatomical specificity.

result: Interneuron manipulation in i/vHP bidirectionally modulates prelimbic activity. Optogenetic activation of Dlx5/6+ interneurons reduces oscillatory power in both i/vHP and PL across frequency bands. Conversely, silencing interneurons with ArchT increases power in both regions (all p<0.001 for i/vHP, p<0.001 for PL theta and gamma).
evaluation: Claims C32-C34 demonstrate bidirectional control with appropriate genetic targeting (Dlx5/6-Cre line). The opposite effects of activation (ChETA) versus silencing (ArchT) provide strong evidence for specificity. Sample sizes are adequate (n=19 for ChETA, n=13 for ArchT). Statistical significance is properly reported, though beta band effect during activation is marginal (p=0.077).

result: Urethane anesthesia reduces oscillatory amplitude and power but preserves network interactions. While anesthesia decreases overall activity levels, firing rate, timing, synchrony, and prefrontal-hippocampal interactions remain similar between anesthetized and non-anesthetized states.
evaluation: Claims C52-C53 address an important methodological consideration. The comparison between anesthetized and non-anesthetized states in the same animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) provides appropriate validation. The preservation of network relationships despite reduced amplitude justifies the use of anesthesia for some experiments, though this is a limitation for interpreting absolute values.

result: A modified three-electrode IUE protocol enables reliable transfection of i/vHP pyramidal neurons. Standard two-electrode IUE successfully targets dHP in >50% of pups but completely fails to target i/vHP (0/32 mice). The three-electrode configuration allows reliable i/vHP transfection, though it is more complex and time-consuming.
evaluation: Claims C76-C78 describe critical methodological development. The complete failure of two-electrode approach for i/vHP (0/32 mice) and success of three-electrode method is clearly documented. This technical advance was essential for the causal experiments. The acknowledgment of increased complexity is appropriate.

result: Despite stronger theta and ripple power in dorsal hippocampus, the prefrontal cortex is mainly coupled with intermediate/ventral hippocampus through phase-locking of neuronal firing via dense direct axonal projections. Theta band-confined optogenetic activation of i/vHP, but not dHP, pyramidal neurons boosts prefrontal oscillations.
evaluation: Claims C36-C37 represent the main conclusions integrating multiple lines of evidence (electrophysiology, anatomy, optogenetics). The apparent paradox—stronger theta in dHP but stronger coupling with i/vHP—is resolved by demonstrating denser anatomical projections and causal optogenetic effects. This synthesis is well-supported by the grouped claims.

result: High-frequency optogenetic stimulation (>16 Hz) fails to evoke precisely timed firing, likely due to neuronal immaturity. Rhythmic prelimbic firing is not detected after hippocampal stimulation, possibly due to sparse axonal projections.
evaluation: Claims C88-C89 describe negative findings with speculative explanations. While the observations are clearly stated, the proposed mechanisms (neuronal immaturity, sparse projections) are not directly tested. These are reasonable interpretations but remain speculative. The lack of rhythmic prelimbic firing is an important observation that constrains mechanistic interpretation.

result: Proposed mechanisms for observed differences include differential cholinergic innervation, maturational differences in intrinsic neuronal properties, parvalbumin gradients, and HCN channel-mediated resonance at 8 Hz.
evaluation: Claims C61, C62, and C72 propose mechanisms based on cited literature but do not provide direct experimental evidence. These are reasonable hypotheses supported by prior work, but they remain speculative in the context of this study. The frequency-specificity of 8 Hz stimulation (C72) is an interesting observation that warrants further investigation.

result: The authors propose that precisely timed excitatory inputs from i/vHP to PL facilitate wiring of prefrontal circuitry through activity-dependent plasticity, acting as a template with pre-adaptive function for future cognitive abilities.
evaluation: Claims C82-C83 present a developmental hypothesis based on general principles of activity-dependent plasticity. While conceptually appealing and grounded in established principles (cited references), this functional interpretation is not directly tested. The study demonstrates early coupling but does not assess long-term consequences for circuit maturation or behavior. This remains an important hypothesis requiring future testing.
